# Even Michael Has a Point

[Silas Bambil · November 2024]{.meta}

I disagree with Michael on so many things. He tends to have rather radical opinions about almost everything, and he is also a stupid boy. But on this particular occasion, I must admit that he has a point. In the lead-up to Ghana's 2024 general election, Michael expressed his frustration with people who continued to defend the New Patriotic Party (NPP) despite conduct he believed had been detrimental to Ghana. Although I did not necessarily subscribe to every aspect of his political assessment, I understood the frustration underlying his argument. It concerned something that bothers me enormously: the willingness of people to excuse wrongdoing simply because it involves people they support.

One of the things I try to be conscious of in my disagreements with Michael is the possibility that he might occasionally be right. Having disagreed with somebody on numerous occasions does not provide sufficient grounds for dismissing everything they subsequently say. I could disagree with nine things Michael says without allowing those disagreements to determine my assessment of the tenth. Besides, there would be little point in accusing him of being unreasonable if I were subsequently unwilling to acknowledge the occasions on which he was reasonable. A good argument does not become a bad one simply because it has had the unfortunate experience of being made by Michael.

What I appreciated about his argument was the distinction between supporting somebody and enabling their wrongdoing. I do not believe that supporting an individual, an institution, or a political party requires me to defend everything they do. If anything, my interest in their success should give me additional reasons to question behaviour that might undermine it. I find it difficult to understand how continually excusing someone's shortcomings is supposed to make them better. Surely, if I genuinely want an institution to improve, I should be interested in whether it recognises its mistakes rather than in how successfully it can persuade people that it has made none.

My only reservation about such arguments is that I want the standards being advocated to remain applicable when the people involved change. If I consider certain conduct unacceptable when it involves the NPP, I should be willing to question comparable conduct when it involves the NDC. That does not mean I consider every political party equally responsible for every problem Ghana faces. It simply means that my assessment of wrongdoing should not depend entirely on the political affiliation of the person responsible for it. I would find it rather inconvenient to possess principles that require me to establish somebody's political affiliation before deciding whether their behaviour is acceptable.

I have no difficulty appreciating why people support particular political parties. People have different experiences, priorities, ideological convictions, and expectations about what constitutes good governance. What I find disturbing is when those preferences begin to determine what people are willing to acknowledge as wrongdoing. An argument that someone would ordinarily find convincing suddenly becomes objectionable because it concerns a party they support. Conduct they would have condemned under different circumstances becomes something they feel compelled to justify. At that point, I begin to wonder whether their political convictions influence their judgement or whether their political affiliations have simply relieved them of the responsibility of exercising it.

For me, the distinction between wanting a political party to succeed and wanting Ghana to succeed is particularly important. My ambitions for Ghana concern the opportunities available to its people, the quality of its institutions, the management of its resources, and the ability of ordinary Ghanaians to build comfortable lives. None of these things becomes less important to me because a different political party assumes office. I would find it unfortunate if my satisfaction with Ghana's progress depended on who received credit for it. Equally, I would find it difficult to celebrate the success of a political organisation if that success did not translate into something meaningful for the country I love.

Of course, this expectation of accountability extends well beyond politics. I expect it from my friends, the people I work with, and, perhaps most importantly, myself. I have made mistakes, exercised poor judgement, and defended positions that I subsequently reconsidered. I cannot reasonably demand that other people acknowledge their shortcomings while continually finding reasons to excuse my own. Neither can I expect my friends to defend everything I do simply because they care about me. I would rather have people in my life who value me enough to tell me when I am wrong than people whose affection for me requires them to pretend that I never am.

I also recognise that I am not entirely immune to the behaviour I criticise. There are people whose opinions I am naturally more inclined to find convincing and others whose opinions I approach with considerable scepticism. Michael, rather amusingly, tends to fall into the latter category. But I want to remain conscious of the possibility that my impression of somebody can influence my assessment of what they say. I do not want to become so comfortable with my own opinions that I reject a reasonable argument simply because acknowledging it would require me to reconsider my position or concede that somebody else had understood something better than I had.

Perhaps that is one of the things I appreciate about being able to disagree with somebody without allowing those disagreements to become the entirety of our relationship. I can find Michael's opinions unnecessarily radical on one occasion and genuinely insightful on another. I do not need to adopt his entire worldview to acknowledge the merits of a particular argument he makes. Nor does agreeing with him on this occasion oblige me to defend whatever he decides to say tomorrow. I am quite certain we will find considerably more things to disagree about, and knowing Michael, I suspect I will not have to wait very long.

Nevertheless, on this particular occasion, I believe his frustration was justified. I would have found it hypocritical to dismiss an argument about independent judgement and accountability simply because Michael happened to be the person making it. After all, what would that say about my own willingness to apply the principles I claim to value? Michael may be a stupid boy, and I reserve the right to remind him of that whenever circumstances require it. But even Michael has a point sometimes. And I would be rather stupid myself if I refused to acknowledge it.

*The original reflection that inspired this essay was written in the lead-up to Ghana's 2024 general election.*
